content.text:
Assuming you mean **the first artificial satellite vs. a very recent modern satellite**, here’s a simple comparison:

| Feature | **First satellite: Sputnik 1** | **Modern/latest satellites** |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Launched** | October 4, 1957 | Continually launched; new ones go up almost every week |
| **Country/company** | Soviet Union | Governments + private companies like SpaceX, Amazon, ESA, China, etc. |
| **Size** | About 58 cm wide — like a beach ball | Can range from tiny CubeSats to bus-sized spacecraft |
| **Mass** | 83.6 kg / 184 lb | From a few kg to several tons |
| **Main job** | Sent simple radio “beep” signals | Internet, GPS, Earth imaging, weather, defense, science, communications |
| **Technology** | Basic radio transmitter + batteries | Solar panels, computers, cameras, AI processing, propulsion, encryption, laser links |
| **Lifetime** | About 3 months in orbit | Months to 15+ years depending on mission |
| **Orbit** | Low Earth orbit | Low, medium, geostationary, lunar, deep-space orbits |
| **Impact** | Started the Space Age | Powers modern life: navigation, phones, internet, weather forecasting, climate monitoring |

**Sputnik 1** was the world’s first artificial satellite, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**; NASA describes it as about **58 cm / 22.8 in** wide, **83.6 kg / 183.9 lb**, and orbiting Earth in about **98 minutes**. ([nasa.gov](https://www.nasa.gov/history/dawn-of-the-space-age/?utm_source=openai))

For “latest,” the exact answer changes constantly. As of **June 8, 2026**, recent/current satellite activity includes missions such as SpaceX/Starlink-related launches and Amazon Leo broadband satellite launches; for example, a listed SpaceX mission on **June 7, 2026** carried classified Starshield-type payloads, while Arianespace announced a planned **June 17, 2026** Ariane 6 launch carrying **36 Amazon Leo satellites**. ([new.nextspaceflight.com](https://new.nextspaceflight.com/launches/details/8264/?utm_source=openai))

**In short:** Sputnik 1 was a simple metal sphere that proved satellites were possible; today’s satellites are powerful space computers that provide internet, navigation, weather data, surveillance, and global communications.
